Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:17: Further, the ways of repentance we learn from Ahab's repentance, as explained in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (ch. 42), in these words: Rabbi Akiva says, repentance was created, and the right hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, is stretched out to receive the penitent every day, and He says, return, children of man. Know the power of charity and repentance — come and see, from Ahab king of Israel, who performed great repentance, for he robbed and stole and murdered, as it is said (I Kings 21:19), "have you murdered and also inherited?" — and he sent and called for Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and he would receive forty lashes from him three times each day, and in fasting and prayer he would rise early and stay late before the Holy One, blessed be He, and he engaged in Torah all his days, and never returned to his evil deeds again, and his repentance was accepted, as it is said (ibid. 21:29), "have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before Me," etc. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:18: Further they said in the Pesikta (DeRav Kahana, piska 24), regarding Ahab's repentance: he had been accustomed to eat at the third hour of the day, and now ate at the fourth hour; at the seventh hour, he ate at the ninth hour. And so they said in the Pesikta (ibid.), "and he went softly" (I Kings 21:27), that he walked barefoot — and we have quoted this above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:19: Further, the ways of repentance we learn from the repentance of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish. It says there in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer: Ben Azzai says, come and see the power of repentance from Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, who, together with his two companions, used to rob and steal from all who passed by them on the road. What did he do? He left his two robber companions in the mountains and returned to the God of his fathers with all his heart, in fasting and prayer, and would rise early and stay late before the Holy One, blessed be He, and engaged in Torah all his days and in gifts to the poor, and never returned to his evil deeds again, and his repentance was accepted; and on the day he died, his robber companions also died in the mountains, and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish was given a portion in life, while his two companions went to the lowest depths of Sheol. Both of them said before the Holy One, blessed be He, is there favoritism before You? This one was a robber together with us in the mountains, and he is in the treasury of life, while we are in the lowest depths of Sheol! He said to them, this one performed repentance in his lifetime, and you did not. They said to him, allow us now, and we will repent. He said to them, there is no repentance except until death. To what may this be compared? To a person who wishes to set sail on the sea — if he does not take with him, from an inhabited land, bread, he will find none at sea; if he wishes to go to the edge of the desert, if he does not take with him, from a settlement, bread and water, in the desert he will find nothing to eat and drink. So too, if a person does not perform repentance in his lifetime, after death he has no repentance, as it is said, "who will not show favoritism," and it is written (Proverbs 6:35), "he will not regard any ransom," and it is written (Jeremiah 17:10), "I, the Lord, search the heart, I test the kidneys." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:20: We learn from the totality of Reish Lakish's repentance five things needed for repentance: first, fasting; second, prayer; third, rising early and staying late at the synagogue; fourth, engaging in Torah; fifth, charity. And these matters, when some of them combine with others, atone for sins and tear up one's decree.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:21: Fasting is fitting for repentance, as it is written (Joel 2:12), "return to Me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:22: Likewise, prayer is needed for repentance — prayer from the depth of the heart — and so it is explained in the Zohar (parashat Acharei Mot, end of p. 69), on the verse (Psalms 130:1), "out of the depths I have called You, O Lord" — it says, when is a person purified from his sin? At the moment he enters into this repentance properly. Rabbi Yitzchak said, that he return before the Supernal King and pray a prayer from the depth of his heart — this being what is written, "out of the depths I have called You, O Lord." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:23: Further, in Vayikra Rabbah (10:5), the Tannaim dispute this: Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi's son said, prayer accomplishes everything — from whom do you learn this? From Hezekiah — his original reign was only fourteen years, as it is said (II Kings 18:13), "and in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah" — and once he prayed, fifteen years were added to him, as it is said (Isaiah 38:5), "behold, I will add to your days fifteen years." Rabbi Yehoshua says, prayer accomplishes half — from whom do you learn this? From Aaron, against whom a harsh decree was issued, as it is said (Deuteronomy 9:20), "and the Lord was very angry with Aaron, to destroy him" — and "destruction" [hashmadah] refers only to the cutting off of children, as it is said (Amos 2:9), "and I destroyed his fruit above and his roots beneath" — and once Moses prayed, two [of Aaron's sons] died and two remained. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:24: Further, on the greatness of prayer, they elaborated at length in Tractate Berachot (32b), in these words: Rabbi Elazar said, prayer is greater than good deeds, for there was none greater in good deeds than Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, and yet he was not answered except through prayer, as it is said (Deuteronomy 3:26), "speak no more to Me of this matter," and immediately following it, "go up to the top of Pisgah." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:25: In Vayikra Rabbah (30:3), on the verse "and you shall take for yourselves on the first day" (Leviticus 23:40), it explains the verse (Psalms 102:18), "He has turned to the prayer of the destitute," as referring to the prayer of Manasseh; and it further says: Rabbi Yitzchak explains the verse regarding these generations, who have neither king, nor prophet, nor priest, nor Urim and Tummim, and have only this prayer alone. David said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the universe, do not despise their prayer. "Let this be written for the last generation" — from here we learn that the Holy One, blessed be He, accepts the penitent. "And a people yet to be created shall praise the Lord" — for the Holy One, blessed be He, creates them as a new creature. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:26: In the Yerushalmi (Rosh Hashanah, ch. 2, halachah 5), regarding the sons of Eli, of whom it is said (I Samuel 3:14), "if it can be atoned," etc., "with sacrifice or offering" — it is explained there that with sacrifice and offering it cannot be atoned, but it can be atoned through prayer.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:27: "Rising early and staying late at the synagogue" — it says in Tanna Devei Eliyahu (Rabbah, ch. 21), on the verse (Numbers 24:6), "like streams stretched out, like gardens by the river" — what is the connection between streams and synagogues and study halls? Rather, just as with these streams, people descend into them impure and immerse and come up pure, so with synagogues and study halls, people enter them full of sins and leave full of commandments. — end of quotation. There are further many greater merits of rising early and staying late, which will be explained in their place, with God's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:28: Torah atones for sin — this is well known. So too charity, among the commandments of acts of lovingkindness, and it is written (Proverbs 16:6), "through kindness and truth, iniquity is atoned for" — and they said in Rosh Hashanah (18a) that even a decree accompanied by an oath is annulled through engaging in Torah and acts of lovingkindness, in these words: with sacrifice and offering it is not atoned, but it is atoned through Torah and acts of lovingkindness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:29: Further they said in Vayikra Rabbah (parashah 25), on the verse "and you shall plant every food-tree" (Leviticus 19:23), in these words: Rav Huna said, if a person stumbled in a transgression liable to death at the hand of Heaven, what should he do to live? If he was accustomed to reading one page [of Scripture], let him read two pages; if he was accustomed to studying one chapter [of Mishnah], let him study two chapters. And if he is not accustomed to reading and studying, what should he do to live? Let him go and become an administrator for the community and a treasurer of charity, and he shall live — for had it been said, "cursed be he who does not study," there would be no way to survive; rather, "cursed be he who does not fulfill" (Deuteronomy 27:26). Had it been said, "it is a tree of life to those who labor in it," there would be no way to survive; rather (Proverbs 3:18), "it is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it." — end of quotation. Here, these two attributes were in Reish Lakish, which are the essence of atoning for sins, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:30: Further, these matters mentioned diminish a person's decree — and so they said in Midrash Kohelet (5:4), on "for in the multitude of dreams and vanities and many words, but fear God" (Ecclesiastes 5:6): Rabbi said, if you have seen harsh dreams and harsh, disturbing visions, or you fear them, hasten to three things and you will be saved — for Rabbi Yudan said in the name of Rabbi Eliezer, three things annul evil decrees: prayer, charity, and repentance, and all three are in one verse (II Chronicles 7:14), "and My people, who are called by My name, humble themselves and pray and seek My face and turn from their evil ways, then I will hear from heaven and forgive their sin." "And they pray" — this is prayer. "And seek My face" — this is charity, this being what is written (Psalms 17:15), "I, in righteousness, shall behold Your face." "And turn from their evil ways" — this is repentance; and afterward, "then I will hear from heaven." Rabbi Muna says, also fasting, as it is said (Psalms 20:2), "may the Lord answer you in the day of trouble." Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yosi say, also changing one's name, changing one's deeds, and changing one's place. — end of quotation, as pertains here; and all these are proven there from verses, and this passage is brought in Bereishit Rabbah (parashah 44:12).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:31: They said (Rosh Hashanah 16b): four things tear up a person's decree: charity, crying out [in prayer], change of name, and change of deed. Crying out, as it is written (Psalms 107:6), "and they cried out to the Lord in their distress, and He delivered them from their afflictions." Charity, as it is written (Proverbs 10:2), "and charity delivers from death." Change of name — as it is written (Jonah 3:10), "and God saw their deeds" [alt.: change of name applies to Abraham/Sarah, but here linked to deeds]. And some say, also change of place. — end of quotation, as pertains here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:32: A penitent must increase charity, as it is said (Daniel 4:24), "and redeem your sin with charity" — the reason being that corresponding to what he diminished the supernal flow, he must increase it, especially on a fast day, as it is written in Isaiah (58:7), "is it not to share your bread with the hungry," etc. — and this refers to the fast.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:33: Further, for repentance sackcloth is needed, as David the king, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 69:12), "and I made sackcloth my clothing." And in Bereishit Rabbah, parashat Vayeshev (parashah 84), our sages, of blessed memory, said on "and Reuben returned to the pit" — and where had he been? Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua [disagree]: Rabbi Eliezer says, engaged in his sackcloth and his fast; when he had finished, he went and peered into that pit — this being what is written (Genesis 37:29), "and Reuben returned to the pit." Rabbi Yehoshua says, all the household burdens were placed upon him, and when he was free of his household burdens, he went and peered into that pit — this being what is written, "and Reuben returned to the pit." The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, never has a person sinned before Me and performed repentance, and you have opened repentance first — by your life, your grandson shall stand and open repentance first — and who is this? This is Hosea, as it is said (Hosea 14:2), "return, O Israel, to the Lord your God." And Rabbi Eliezer's words are more strongly confirmed in the Zohar. Here, repentance is with fasting and sackcloth.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:34: Further there, Rabbi Abahu said, because our father Jacob grasped sackcloth, it has never departed from his sons and his sons' sons until the end of all generations, though it applies only to great men: David, as it is said (I Chronicles 21:16), "and David and the elders fell, covered with sackcloth"; Ahab, "and he put sackcloth on his flesh" (I Kings 21:27); Jehoram, "and the people saw, and behold, sackcloth was on his flesh" (II Kings 6:30); Mordechai, "and he put on sackcloth and ashes" (Esther 4:1). — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:35: Further, in Bereishit Rabbah, on the verse "and it came to pass at that time that Judah went down" (parashah 85), in these words: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani opened, "for I know the thoughts" (Jeremiah 29:11) — the tribes were engaged with the sale of Joseph, while Joseph was engaged in his sackcloth and his fast, Reuben was engaged in his sackcloth and his fast, and Jacob was engaged in his sackcloth and his fast. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:36: Further, in Midrash Rabbah, parashat Vezot HaBerachah, they say, in these words: when Moses saw that a decree had been sealed against him, he decreed a fast, and drew a small circle and stood within it, and said, I will not move from here until that decree is annulled. At that moment, what did Moses do? He put on sackcloth and wrapped himself in sackcloth and rolled in ashes, and stood in prayer and supplication before the Omnipresent, until heaven and earth and the order of creation trembled. — end of quotation, as pertains here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:37: Further they said in the Midrash (Yalkut, Esther, siman 1056), on the verse (Esther 4:4), "and she sent garments to clothe Mordechai and to remove his sackcloth from him, but he did not accept them" — in these words: he said, I will not remove the sackcloth until the Holy One, blessed be He, performs miracles for me as He did for those before me — for Jacob it is written, "and he put sackcloth on his loins"; and for Ahab, it did not last more than three years; and likewise for Jehoram, his sackcloth did not end until the famine of Samaria [was resolved].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:38: I have heard from the Kabbalists that "SaK" [sackcloth] has the numerical value of four hundred; and the matter is that there are four hundred companies among the kelipot, of which it is said regarding Esau (Genesis 32:6), "and four hundred men with him"; and there are above four hundred worlds of mercy, as explained at the beginning of the Idra (parashat Naso 128b). By donning this sackcloth one merits to subdue the four hundred of the Sitra Achra [Other Side] and to merit, in the World to Come, the four hundred worlds of yearning, which are called "four hundred shekels of silver, current with the merchant."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:39: I have also heard that this is alluded to in the forty-two-letter Name, in its final name, ShaKuTzit — "tzit" in the language of the Targum means "listening"; and the intent is that sackcloth causes the hearing of prayer, and likewise "Sh'ma K'lenu" [hear our voice] has the initial letters Shin-Kof [SaK].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:40: My master, may his rest be in Eden, wrote regarding what is said in Ra'aya Meheimna (parashat Pinchas 227a), that "straw" [kash] and "chaff" [teven] are the kelipot, and "KeSh" reversed is "SaK" — and the intent is that since the penitent sinned and was drawn after the kelipah, it is fitting that he put sackcloth on his flesh, and thereby subdue his inclination, which is the straw.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:41: I say that regarding exile it is said (Isaiah 50:3), "I clothe the heavens with blackness, and I make sackcloth their covering" — the Holy One, blessed be He, of whom it is said (I Kings 8:32), "and You shall hear in heaven," is clothed in sackcloth; and the Shechinah is described (Joel 1:8), "lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth." And since a person, through his sin, has caused them to be clothed more in sackcloth than they should be — for when we sin, we prolong the exile and give the sackcloth, which is the servant [Metatron/the outside forces], more dominion than it deserves — and likewise the whole soul is clothed in sackcloth, which is the kelipah — therefore, for the rectification of the Shechinah and the rectification of his own soul, he should put sackcloth upon himself, especially in days of distress and weeping, when it is fitting to wear sackcloth.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:42: Now, the reason for accepting sufferings, fasting, weeping, and sackcloth is that the penitent, through his sin, caused blemish above, and that darkness depends on the supernal attributes, and through his acceptance of judgment upon himself, he purifies the supernal attributes from their blemish and darkness, for that judgment and darkness descend upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:43: This matter we learn from the first man — for once he knew what he had blemished, he accepted upon himself the decree of judgment, and the supernal attributes were purified. There is proof for this in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 69, 99a), where it says (Genesis 4:1), "and the man knew Eve his wife" — and until now Adam did not know his wife — but rather, at the time he sinned, the Shechinah departed from her place, and thus the masters of the Mishnah have established, that at a time when the Shechinah is not in her place, marital relations are forbidden, etc. — and it was he who caused that bed to depart from there, thus he departed from marital relations; and after he accepted his punishment, the bed returned to its place at that time — "and the man knew Eve his wife." — end of quotation. Here it is explicitly stated that when he accepted upon himself the decree of his punishment, the attributes were rectified.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:44: My master, may his rest be in Eden, used to say that on this matter they instituted in the confession, "and You are righteous concerning all that has come upon me, for You have acted truthfully, and I have acted wickedly" — the intent being that in confessing his sin, he purifies the supernal attributes and brings down the darkness and blemish, which is the judgment, upon himself — this being "and You are righteous concerning all that has come [upon me]," "has come" meaning what has come and what will come. "For You have acted truthfully" — meaning, in the bestowal of the judgment that will come, the attribute of Truth [Emet] is rectified, and he acted wickedly and it is fitting for it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:45: Another reason for accepting sufferings is that whoever transgresses a single sin acquires for himself an accuser [kateigor] who stands and accuses him forever; and when a person confesses, that accuser is removed from before him and does not accuse — and so it is explained in the Zohar (parashat Kedoshim 83b) regarding David, when he said "I have sinned," and the prophet said to him (II Samuel 12:13), "also the Lord has removed your sin, you shall not die" — for the matter is difficult: if the Holy One, blessed be He, had removed his sin, why did David perform so much mortification and fasting? Rather, this is resolved by what is explained there — that the intent is, He removed it from before the Holy One, blessed be He, so that it not accuse him, in these words: come and see, a person who performs a commandment — that commandment ascends and stands before the Holy One, blessed be He, and says, I am the commandment of so-and-so who performed me, and the Holy One, blessed be He, appoints it before Him to watch over him every day, to do good for him for its sake. If he transgressed the words of Torah, that transgression ascends before Him and says, I am the transgression of so-and-so who committed me, and the Holy One, blessed be He, appoints it before Him and it stands there to watch over him, to destroy him — this being what is written (Deuteronomy 32:19), "and the Lord saw and spurned, out of anger with His sons and His daughters" — what is "and He saw"? That which stands before Him. If he returns in repentance, what is written? "Also the Lord has removed your sin, you shall not die" — that He removed that sin from before Him, so that He not look upon it, to do good for him — and therefore it is written (Deuteronomy 9:27), "do not turn to the stubbornness of this people, nor to their wickedness, nor to their sin." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:46: Here, through sin an accuser is created, and therefore one must accept sufferings upon himself to scour away his sins, as it is said (Psalms 89:33), "then I will punish their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with plagues" — and through this his sins are atoned for.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:47: It seems to me that for the reason our sages, of blessed memory, said (Avot 4:11), that whoever transgresses a single sin acquires an accuser for himself, one may understand why Onkelos translates "chet" [sin] as "chova" [debt] (Numbers 18:22), "chatatam" as "chovayhon" (Exodus 32:32) — that the sin, which is an accuser, is a debt for a person, which he is obligated to pay off — for in committing the sin he borrows what is not his; for a person's nature is to be in holiness, and when he follows the counsels of his inclination, he owes it for what he enjoyed from it. And how does he pay it off? By returning what he enjoyed from it through the scouring of sufferings. And just as Gehinnom, the accusing power he created through his sin, comes and takes its vengeance upon him — in the manner explained in the Zohar, parashat Korach (177a), "a man's deed shall be repaid to him," etc. (Job 34:11) — so, in order to scour away the impure power he drew upon his soul, in this world too that impure power is scoured through the acceptance of sufferings, and when he completes the scouring, that accuser is nullified, in the manner they said (Sotah 9a), "His arrows are consumed," etc. — for arrows are only to fulfill the will of the one who shoots them, and once the commands are carried out, they are nullified — and this is (Isaiah 44:22), "I have wiped away your transgressions like a thick cloud," etc., "return to Me, for I have redeemed you" — the intent being, I have redeemed you from those debts you were held by.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:48: Therefore one must accept sufferings with love and not rebel against them; and so they expounded in the Mechilta (parashat Yitro), on the verse (Exodus 20:20), "do not make [gods] with Me" [alt. "do not do thus to Me"] — in these words: Rabbi Akiva says, "do not do thus to Me" — do not treat Me as others treat their gods — that when good comes upon them, they honor their gods, as it is said (Habakkuk 1:16), "therefore he sacrifices to his net," and when calamity comes upon them, they curse their gods, as it is said (Isaiah 8:21), "and it shall come to pass, when he is hungry," etc., "and curses by his king." But rather, if I bring good upon you, give thanks, and if I bring sufferings upon you, give thanks — and so David said (Psalms 116:13), "I will raise the cup of salvations, and call upon the name of the Lord," (ibid. 116:3-4), "distress and sorrow I found, and I called upon the name of the Lord." And so Job said (Job 1:21), "the Lord has given, and the Lord has taken away, blessed be the name of the Lord" — regarding both the state of good and the state of calamity; and so Job's wife said to him (ibid. 2:9), "do you still hold fast to your integrity?" — and what did he say to her? "You speak as one of the base women speaks." The people of the generation of the Flood and the people of Sodom, who were accustomed to good, when calamity came upon them, accepted it against their will — but we, who were fitting in good, are not fitting in calamity. Further, one should be more joyful in sufferings than in good, for even a person who has had good all his days is not forgiven for the transgressions in his hand — and who forgives him? You must say, sufferings.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:49: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says, behold it says (Proverbs 3:11), "do not despise the discipline of the Lord, my son" — why? "For whom the Lord loves, He rebukes." You might say, go and see, what caused this son to please his father? You must say, this is sufferings. Rabbi Meir says (Deuteronomy 8:5), "and you shall know in your heart, that as a man disciplines his son" — you should know the deeds you have done, and the sufferings I have brought upon you — for I have not brought sufferings upon you according to your deeds.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:50: Rabbi Natan says, sufferings are beloved — for just as a covenant is made regarding the land, so a covenant is made regarding sufferings, as it is said (Deuteronomy 8:5), "the Lord your God disciplines you," and it says, "for the Lord your God brings you into a good land." Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says, sufferings are beloved — for the Holy One, blessed be He, gave Israel three precious gifts, and they were given only through sufferings, and these are: Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come. Torah, from where? As it is said (Proverbs 1:2), "to know wisdom and discipline, to understand words of understanding," and it is written (Psalms 94:12), "happy is the man whom You discipline, O Lord, and teach him from Your Torah." The Land of Israel, from where? Scripture teaches, "the Lord your God disciplines you," and it says, "for the Lord your God brings you into a good land." The World to Come, from where? Scripture teaches (Proverbs 6:23), "for the commandment is a lamp, and the Torah is light, and the way of life is the reproofs of discipline" — go and see, which way brings a person to the life of the World to Come? You must say, this is sufferings.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:51: Rabbi Nechemyah says, sufferings are beloved — for just as sacrifices appease, so sufferings appease. Regarding sacrifices, what does it say (Leviticus 1:4), "and it shall be accepted for him, to atone for him"; regarding sufferings, what does it say (ibid. 26:43), "and they shall accept [appease for] their iniquity"? And not only that, but sufferings appease more than sacrifices, because sacrifices are with money, but sufferings are with the body — and so it says (Job 2:4), "skin for skin, and all that a man has [he will give for his life]." They further expounded there on the greatness of sufferings, that although Hezekiah taught Manasseh Torah, this availed him nothing — only sufferings did, as it is said (II Chronicles 33:12), "and when he was in distress, he entreated the favor of the Lord" — thus you learn that sufferings are beloved. — end of quotation. Here is the greatness of sufferings, that they atone for a person's sins, etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:52: Likewise, our sages, of blessed memory, expounded (Berachot 5a), in these words: and this is what Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish [said] — a covenant was made regarding salt, and a covenant was made regarding sufferings. A covenant was made regarding salt, as it is written (Leviticus 2:13), "and you shall not omit the salt of the covenant of your God"; and a covenant was made regarding sufferings (Deuteronomy 28:69), "these are the words of the covenant." Just as the covenant mentioned regarding salt — salt sweetens the meat — so the covenant mentioned regarding sufferings: sufferings scour away all a person's sins. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:53: There, in Berachot, after this passage, the passage of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai is also brought — three gifts the Holy One, blessed be He, gave to Israel. Since this has come to our hands, let us say something about it: these three gifts may be said to correspond to nefesh, ru'ach, neshamah, and it is known that the root of these is placed in the attributes; and the reason Torah is mentioned before the Land of Israel is that Israel, before they merited the gift of the Land of Israel, merited the gift of the Torah in the wilderness, and before they merited it, there were sufferings — first (Exodus 14:10), "and Pharaoh drew near, and the children of Israel lifted up their eyes," and then the splitting of the Sea of Reeds, "and they came to Marah and could not drink the waters of Marah" (ibid. 15:23), and afterward at Rephidim, "and the people thirsted there for water" (ibid. 17:3), and afterward Amalek. And likewise, before they entered the Land, Sichon and Og came against them. Likewise, in the World to Come, a river of fire flows and issues forth from before Him (Daniel 7:10), and it is explained in the Tikkunim (4a) that souls immerse in it, etc.; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:54: The reason they were given through sufferings is that they are three [manifestations of] "Elohim," as explained in the Zohar (parashat Bereishit 31b), in these words: Rabbi Yosi said, what is meant by (Deuteronomy 4:7), "which has God near to it"? "Near" [karovim, plural] — it should have said "karov" [singular]! Rather, the supernal Elohim, the Elohim of "the Fear of Isaac" [Gevurah], and the final Elohim — and therefore "near" [plural] — and many mighty acts emerge from one, and all are one. — end of quotation. Now, the Torah was given in fire, which is the second Elohim, "the Fear of Isaac"; and likewise the Land of Israel is the final Elohim, and the attribute of Righteousness [Tzedek] lodges in it. And likewise the World to Come, which is the supernal Elohim. Therefore they must necessarily come through sufferings, so that that judgment be poured out below and sweetened on the side of Chesed after the acceptance of judgment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:55: They said they were given only through sufferings — for even a perfectly righteous person needs sufferings to merit them. So too we find that the Rashbi, peace be upon him, did not merit his wondrous wisdom except through the sufferings he endured in the cave for thirteen years, as explained in parashat Bereishit (Zohar 11b), and likewise in Tractate Shabbat (33b). The reason, as explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (parashat Pinchas 247a), which we quoted in the Gate of Holiness (ch. 15), where he said: further, there is a secret [mixed] with beaten oil — surely the Torah is not "beaten" [mixed properly] except for one who endures several beatings for its sake, as the masters of the Mishnah have established, that Torah is sustained only in one who kills himself over it. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:56: This allusion is alluded to in the Torah in another place, where it says (Exodus 27:20), "and they shall take for you pure olive oil, beaten, for the light" — for pure olive oil, which is the Torah, does not give light except through beating, which is the beating of matter — how much more so one who has sins, for in order to purify the blemish of the supernal attributes and the blemish of his soul, he must accept sufferings, so that he merit the World to Come or merit Torah.
